# Plots with ggplot2 {#sec-ggplot}

```{r}
#| label: setup-ggplot
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
load_steps("code/4_ggplot_basics.r", "ggplot")
```

This chapter teaches ggplot2 on the same trial data. It starts with the basic plot types and then dresses one plot up until it is ready for a paper.

ggplot2 builds a plot in layers. You start with the data and say which column goes on which axis. Then you add a layer that draws, a layer that names things and a layer that sets the look. Each layer is joined with `+`.

The script is `code/4_ggplot_basics.r`.

## Step 1: packages and paths

Three packages. `dplyr` gets the data ready, `ggplot2` draws, and `ragg` saves the final figure as a TIFF.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-1
#| message: false
```

## Step 2: the data for the plots

Two small tables are made first. `df_base` has one row per patient. `df_mean` has one row per arm per month, with the mean and the standard deviation (SD) of FBS. The line plot and the bar graph of means are drawn from `df_mean`.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-2
```

## Step 3: a first scatter plot

Every plot needs three things. The data, `aes()` to say which column goes on each axis, and a geom to draw it. `geom_point()` draws one dot per row, so here one dot per patient.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-3
```

## Step 4: colour the dots by a third variable

Add one more column to `aes()` and ggplot2 colours the dots by it. It also draws the legend for you. `alpha` makes the dots see-through, so dots that overlap look darker.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-4
```

## Step 5: a line plot

A line joins the points in the order of x. Each arm needs its own line. `group = treatment` says which points belong together and `colour = treatment` gives each line its own colour.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-5
```

## Step 6: a loess curve

`geom_smooth()` draws a fitted curve over the raw points. A loess curve is a flexible local fit. It follows the data without a shape chosen in advance, so it is a good first look. The grey band is the 95% confidence interval.

The x axis is `time_months`, the exact time of each visit, so the dots spread out instead of sitting in five columns.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-6
```

## Step 7: a straight line, the linear fit

`method = "lm"` fits a linear regression and draws it as a straight line. FBS falls fast at first and then levels off. A straight line cannot bend, so it misses that shape. Compare it with the loess curve above.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-7
```

## Step 8: curved fits, quadratic and cubic

The fit is still `lm`, but the formula now has a curve in it. `poly(x, 2)` adds x squared, which gives one bend. `poly(x, 3)` adds x cubed as well, which allows two bends.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-8
```

## Step 9: all four fits on one plot

Several `geom_smooth()` layers can share one plot. Writing `colour = "Linear"` inside `aes()` gives each line a name, so the legend lists them all. The loess, quadratic and cubic curves follow the levelling off. The straight line does not.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-9
```

## Step 10: bar graphs

There are two bar geoms. `geom_bar()` counts the rows for you. `geom_col()` draws a height you already worked out, here the mean FBS. `position = "dodge"` puts the two arms side by side instead of stacking them.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-10
```

## Step 11: change the theme, theme_classic

A theme changes the look, never the data. The default has a grey panel and a white grid. `theme_classic()` is the usual choice for a paper. It has a white background, an x and a y axis line with ticks, and no grid.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-11
```

## Step 12: add the axis lines and ticks yourself

`theme_minimal()` has no axis lines and no ticks, so it is a good place to learn how to add them. `axis.line` draws the axes, `axis.ticks` draws the ticks and `axis.ticks.length` sets their length.

The scale sets where the ticks go. `breaks` puts a tick at each visit, and `limits` sets the range. Minor ticks are the small unlabelled ticks in between.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-12
```

## Step 13: name the axes, the legend and the plot

`labs()` names everything in one place. The legend is named after the aesthetic it shows, here `colour`.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-13
```

## Step 14: bold, size and face of the axis text and the title

`theme()` changes one piece of text at a time. `axis.text` is the numbers on the axes and `axis.title` is the axis names. `face` can be plain, bold, italic or bold.italic, and `size` is in points. Add `.x` or `.y` to change one axis only.

The theme is kept in an object called `bold_text`, so it can be added to any later plot with one `+`.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-14
```

## Step 15: dodge the points so the arms do not overlap

At each month the two arms sit at almost the same height, so their points and error bars cover each other. `position_dodge()` moves each arm a little to the side. Every layer that must move together gets the same dodge.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-15
```

## Step 16: dodge the raw points too

With one dot per patient, the arms also land on top of each other. `position_jitterdodge()` first puts the arms side by side and then spreads each arm's dots a little sideways. Now every patient can be seen.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-16
```

## Step 17: save the finished figure

`ggsave()` writes a plot to a file. Journals usually want a TIFF at 300 dpi. `ragg::agg_tiff` stores the 300 dpi inside the file, and width and height are in inches.

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-step-17
```
